summary: A 1917 steel tower near Cherry Springs, rebuilt by CCC crews in 1938; still standing but out of fire service, with climbing access unconfirmed.

facts.design: Steel frame fire tower; the 1917 tower was bought from Aermotor, and the maker of the 1938 replacement is not stated
facts.status_note: Still stands but is no longer used to detect fires, because forest growth now blocks the view.

access.note: Entrance is off PA 44 about two miles south of Cherry Springs State Park. No source says whether the steel tower may be climbed; check with the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry first.

visit.trail_note: Susquehannock Trail System orange blazes run near the tower. The CCC stone cabin nearby is used by scouts and the Susquehannock Trail Club.

events.note: New steel tower near Cherry Springs, bought from the Aermotor Company and erected August-September 1917 by the State Forestry Department; height reported as 60 ft
Iron steps erected on the steel tower in June 1918
Telephone line of about 13 miles run from Carter Camp to the tower
Jap Knecht named as watchman at the tower in a Wellsboro Gazette item (December 1924)
CCC enrollees from Camp S-136 built a larger steel frame tower; the Lumber Museum gives 80 ft and says it replaced a 65 ft tower from 1917
Registered April 28, 2017 as US 1193, PA 20, nominated by Brian M. Powell

corrections.why: 18.3 m (60 ft) matches the 1917 tower in the forest warden's report. The Lumber Museum gives the current 1938 tower as 80 ft, about 24.4 m.

corrections.proposed: Steel frame fire tower; the 1917 tower was bought from Aermotor
corrections.why: Aermotor is documented only for the 1917 tower. The sources reached do not name the maker of the 1938 CCC tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1917 forest warden's report says sixty feet and a Wellsboro paper of 1917 planned seventy feet for the 1917 tower. The Lumber Museum says the 1938 tower is 80 ft and the 1917 tower was 65 ft. The story uses the museum figure for the current tower and says the earlier height is uncertain.
The NHLR says a fire tower has stood on the site since 1917, and the 1938 CCC tower replaced the 1917 tower. Both accounts fit: the earlier tower dates to 1917 and the present structure to 1938.

notes_for_editor: Height and build history conflict across sources (60, 65, 70 ft for the 1917 tower; 80 ft for the 1938 tower, given by one source only). Climbing access is unconfirmed: no source states whether the tower may be climbed, so access is 'unknown' and the story says not to climb until the Bureau of Forestry confirms. A social-media post (not cited, not verified) dated the first tower to 1921 and said it stopped being used in the 1990s; the story does not use either claim. The staffing as_of is undated because the Lumber Museum page carries no date. No notable fire is documented in the sources reached.
